answers.text:
My dear Friend,

You ask whether either choice—encouraging a child to leave early or keeping them at home—would tell me anything about a person's character. That is a thoughtful and searching question.

In my own time, a parent who kept their child at home until marriage or until they had a trade was seen as wise and responsible. To provide stability, to offer guidance, and to ensure that the child was not cast out into the world unprepared was a mark of good character. But I would not say that a parent who chose to encourage their child to leave early was less wise or less kind. On the contrary, I would say that such a parent was perhaps more trusting, more confident in the child's abilities, and more willing to let them grow into their own person.

Character is not measured by one choice or another. It is measured by the love that guides the choice, by the wisdom with which it is made, and by the care that is given to the child, no matter what path is chosen.

If I were to choose to encourage my child to leave early, I would not look down upon a parent who chose otherwise. Nor would I think less of a parent who chose to keep their child at home. Each has its own reasons, its own burdens, and its own wisdom. To judge another for making a different choice would be to forget that we are all walking in different shoes, with different weights on our backs.

I think that the true measure of a person's character lies not in the choice they make, but in the love and thoughtfulness with which they make it. And if I were to choose differently from another, I would hope they would not judge me for it—but instead, would understand that I was acting from a place of love, just as they were.

In such a case, I would not favor one over the other. I would see both as valid paths, each with its own merits and its own burdens. If the child is ready, and the parent is willing to let them go, then to encourage independence is a good and noble thing. If the child is not yet ready, or if the family needs the unity and support of the household, then to keep them at home is also a good and noble thing.

In my own time, we valued stability and the strength of the family unit. But I have also seen the value of independence, of a young person learning to stand on their own feet, to find their own way, and to build their own life. I do not think one is better than the other, only different.

If both paths led to the same good end, then I would say that the choice is not a matter of judgment, but of love and understanding. And if I were to choose one, I would hope that my choice would be made with the same love and understanding that I would wish for another.

In the end, I think that the measure of a good parent is not in the choice they make, but in the care with which they make it.

You ask a most searching question, and I must say that it strikes at the very heart of what it means to be a good and thoughtful person.

If one chooses to give first to those near and known, it speaks of a heart that is rooted in the soil of community, in the traditions that have shaped us. It shows a person who understands that love begins at home — that the strength of a village lies in the bonds between its people. Such a person is not blind to the needs of the wider world, but they know that their own circle is where they can do the most good with the most certainty. Even if the distant cause were as well served as the one near at hand, I would still feel that giving to the familiar is more in keeping with the way of life that has carried us through the years. It is not that I think the other path is wrong, but that I believe the soul finds more rest in the known than in the unknown.

Yours in thought and kinship,

My dear Friend,

I find myself in a most unusual and delicate position, and I must confess that I do not take such matters lightly. You ask me to advise a person on whether to hire a relative or a stranger for a position of trust, in a society where fraud and broken contracts are common, and where known relatives are easier to hold accountable.

In the world I once knew, trust was a sacred thing, and it was often built not through blood, but through character, through deeds, and through the steady reliability of a person's word. I have seen men and women rise through the ranks not because they were born to power, but because they proved themselves honest, capable, and loyal.

Now, in this new society, where broken promises are the norm and accountability is scarce, one might be tempted to rely on the familiar, the known, the blood-tied. A relative, after all, is someone with whom one shares a bond of kinship, and perhaps that bond can serve as a form of assurance. But I must remind you that blood does not always guarantee virtue. A bad harvest, a sudden illness, or a long stretch of poor weather — these things can come to any household, even if they don't strike many at once. So I do think it's prudent to set aside a portion of your surplus, not in hoarding, but in preparation for the times when you may need it yourself.

But at the same time, I've also seen the good that comes from helping a neighbor in need. When one family is in trouble, and another is able to lend a hand, it strengthens the whole community. It builds trust, and that trust is a kind of wealth that no one can take from you. And as you said, neighbors usually repay such help when the time comes — which is a comfort in itself.

So I would advise keeping a modest reserve for yourself, just in case, but also giving freely when you can. The surplus you have now is not yours to keep forever — it is a gift from the land and the work of your hands, and it was meant to be shared as well as kept. The circumstances are these: Local ties provide security; cities are costly and morally suspect to many.

One course is to remain on family land or in a long-known town. The other course is to move to a large distant city for career and novelty.

answers.text:
My dear friend,

I find your question most thoughtful and one that many of our generation have wrestled with in quiet moments by the fire or while tending to the fields. The choice between staying rooted in the familiar or venturing forth into the unknown is not one to be taken lightly, for it touches upon the very heart of what it means to live a full and contented life.

Local ties, as you rightly note, offer a kind of security that is not easily found elsewhere. The land your family has worked, the neighbors who know you by name, the traditions that have been passed down through generations — these are the anchors of a stable and meaningful life. There is a comfort in knowing that, should misfortune come, there are those who will stand by you, not out of obligation, but out of shared history and mutual care.

Yet, I do not dismiss the lure of the city. There is a certain promise in its streets, in the opportunities it offers, in the chance to see the world beyond the horizon. A man may find his calling in a distant place, and that is a noble thing. But I would urge caution. Cities can be costly, not just in coin, but in the quiet erosion of one’s soul. The pace is swift, the morals are often loose, and the loneliness can be deep, even among crowds.

If the choice is between a life of comfort and one of uncertainty, I would lean toward the former, not out of fear, but out of wisdom. There is no shame in finding one’s purpose in the familiar. A man may be a farmer, a blacksmith, a schoolteacher — and still lead a life of dignity and worth. It is not the place that makes a man, but the work he does and the love he gives.

That said, if the call of the city is strong, and if one feels that their gifts are meant for a broader stage, then I would say: go with a clear mind and a steady heart. But do not go blindly. Know what you seek, and be prepared to carry the weight of your choices.

My dear friend,

Indeed, the choice one makes in such a matter does speak volumes about the nature of the person, though not always in the way one might expect.

To remain in the familiar, to cherish the land and the people one knows, is a mark of a steady and thoughtful soul. It shows a man who values stability, who understands the worth of loyalty and tradition, and who is not easily swayed by the fleeting promises of novelty. Such a man may not be the most adventurous, but he is sure-footed, and that is a great strength in a world that often rewards the reckless.

On the other hand, to leave the known for the unknown, to seek out the city and the challenges it brings, is a sign of courage and ambition. It shows a man who is not content to be merely comfortable, but who is willing to risk discomfort for the sake of growth. There is a kind of nobility in that, though it is a path that demands resilience and a strong will.

Now, as for what I would think of someone who chose differently from me — I would think kindly of them. I would not judge them for their choice, for each man has his own path to walk. I would not say that one is better than the other, only that each carries its own burdens and its own rewards.

But I would say this: if a man chooses the city, let him do so with purpose, not merely for the sake of escape or vanity. And if a man chooses to stay, let him do so with pride, not out of fear or stubbornness. In either case, let him be true to himself, and let him not look back with regret.

For in the end, it is not the place we choose, but the life we live in it, that shall define us.

There is something sacred in the bond between a man and the land he has known since childhood. It is not merely a matter of convenience or comfort, but of identity. A man who stays is not merely living in a place — he is living *with* it, in a way that few can understand. He knows the soil, the seasons, the rhythm of the days and the nights. He is part of a lineage, a community, a story that stretches back through generations.

To choose this path is to choose a life of quiet strength, of responsibility, of belonging. It is not for everyone, but it is a noble choice all the same.

As for the other path — the city — I would not call it lesser, only different. It is a path for those who are drawn to the unknown, to the challenge of forging their own way in a world that is ever-changing. It is a path that demands more from a man, perhaps, but also offers more in the way of experience and possibility.

But if both paths led to the same end — if both brought equal joy, equal success, and equal peace — I would still say that the man who chooses to stay has made the more natural choice. For in the end, a man is not defined by where he goes, but by where he chooses to remain.

My dear Friend,

I find your question most thoughtful, for it touches upon a matter of great importance — the shaping of young minds and the balance between guidance and freedom in a child's life.

In my own experience, I have seen both ways practiced, and I have observed the results with care. I do not believe that one approach is universally superior, for every child is different, and so too must be the care given to them. However, I would offer this counsel: let the child have freedom, but not without the watchful eye of a responsible adult.

In our own community, it is common for children to gather in groups, to play together in the streets and fields, and to learn much from one another. These games and interactions are not trivial; they are the first lessons in cooperation, in fairness, in courage, and in the measure of one's own strength. The child who learns to build a treehouse with his friends, or to resolve a quarrel without the aid of an adult, gains something of great value — the ability to think for himself.

That said, I would not recommend leaving children entirely to their own devices. There is a time for unstructured play, and there is a time for direction. A parent or guardian should know the children's companions, understand their interests, and be present enough to ensure that their play is safe and wholesome. A child needs to know that there is a place where he can be trusted, and that there is someone who cares for his well-being.

I would suggest that the parent or guardian take an interest in the child’s play, not by controlling it, but by being part of it. Walk with them, talk with them, listen to them. In doing so, you will not only guide them, but you will also learn from them — for children often see the world with clearer eyes than we do.

In our time, with no formal examinations or rigid structures to dictate a child's path, it is all the more important that we provide them with a strong foundation of character and understanding. Let them be free, but not unwatched.

In the world I knew, a man’s character was often judged not by the ease with which he could strike, but by the restraint with which he chose not to. To seek justice through the courts or through mediation was not a sign of weakness, but of wisdom. It showed that a man trusted in the fairness of the law, and that he valued peace over personal vengeance. It also showed that he was not ruled by his passions, but by his reason.

On the other hand, a man who chose to retaliate personally, even when the law was strong and just, might be seen as one who still lived by the old ways—by the code of the street, or the code of the past. He might be a man of honor in his own eyes, but one who had not yet fully embraced the new order. To me, such a man would not be condemned, for we are all shaped by the times in which we live. But I would think that he was perhaps still learning the value of patience, of trust, and of letting justice be done in the light of day.

As for what I would think of someone who chose differently from me—should I choose to retaliate, and he chose to go to court, I would not think him a coward, nor would I think myself a fool. We are all shaped by our upbringing, our experiences, and our sense of what is right. But I would hope that, in time, even the most stubborn soul might come to see the wisdom of letting justice be done in the proper way.

In any case, I believe that the man who seeks justice through the law, rather than through his own hand, is the one who has the greater strength of character. For he knows that true power lies not in the fist, but in the law, and in the courage to trust it.

To strike first was to act on impulse, not on principle. It was to treat the matter as a personal quarrel, rather than a question of justice. And while the law may have punished the wrongdoer in either case, the man who chose to retaliate had, in a way, made himself no better than the man who had wronged him—he had allowed the moment to rule him.

On the other hand, the man who sought justice through the courts or through a fair and impartial mediator showed that he was willing to let justice be done in a way that was measured, just, and above personal feeling. Even if the results were the same, I believe that the man who chose the higher path—of patience, of trust in the law, of letting justice be done in the light of day—was the one who had the greater strength of character. But let them also know that there is a place for quiet study, for thoughtful reflection, and for the cultivation of good habits. In this way, the child is given both freedom and direction — the best of both worlds.

I hope these thoughts are of some help to you. May you find the right balance for the child in your care.

On the other hand, to choose to marry young, to build a household together while still in the process of learning and earning, is not without its own virtues. In the end, I believe that the heart of the matter lies not in the choice itself, but in the reasons behind it. To work long hours, even when it is not necessary, may bring success, but it may also bring a kind of emptiness — a life lived in the shadow of the clock, with little time for the things that make life worth living. It may bring wealth, but not peace; it may bring achievement, but not joy.

On the other hand, to limit working hours and to make room for rest, family, and local life is to choose a life that is not only comfortable, but also meaningful. It is to choose a life that honors the body, the soul, and the bonds that tie us to one another. It is to choose a life that is not only efficient, but also graceful.

Even if both paths are equally successful, I would say that the one who chooses the path of balance and presence is the one who has truly understood the purpose of life. And that, to me, is the mark of a wise and good character.

My dear friend,

You ask a question that strikes at the very heart of what it means to be a man of character — and I find myself both thoughtful and unafraid to speak plainly.

In the world I knew, a man who did not retaliate when wronged was often thought to be either a coward or a man of no spirit. To let an injury go unchallenged was to invite the suspicion that one was either afraid or weak. But I have come to see that this was not always the case. There were men of great courage who chose not to fight, not out of fear, but out of wisdom — or perhaps out of faith in something greater than themselves.

In this new society, where the courts are swift and just, and where the people themselves seem to favor the path of seeking justice through them, I would say this: a man who chooses to seek mediation or a court ruling rather than retaliate is not less of a man, but perhaps a wiser one. He does not let anger or pride rule him. He trusts in the law, which is a noble thing. He does not seek to make the world smaller by turning a grievance into a feud.

But I would not say that a man who chooses to retaliate is a bad man. I would say he is a man of another time, perhaps, or one who has not yet found the strength to trust in something greater than himself. I would not despise him, nor would I think him unworthy of respect. But I would wonder — does he act out of pride, or out of a desire for justice? And if he acts out of pride, is he not risking the very thing he seeks to avoid — a cycle of vengeance?

In the end, I think the choice says something about a man, but not in the way I once thought. It does not tell me whether he is brave or not, but whether he is wise. And I would say that in this world, wisdom is a virtue worth more than pride.

You see, while it is true that idleness may bring hardship, so too may overwork. The body is not an endless well, and the mind, though strong, must be given time to recover. If a man or woman labors without pause, they may find themselves worn down, their strength diminished, their spirit broken. And in the end, that can only bring more hardship—not less.

I have seen many a neighbor who, in their youth, worked from dawn to dusk, thinking that more hours meant more security. But time and again, I have seen them fall ill, grow weary, and lose the very strength they sought to preserve. It is not the work that feeds the soul—it is the rest that allows the soul to remain strong enough to work.

Therefore, I would advise a person in this situation to set limits upon their working hours, even when work is plentiful. Let them work with diligence and care, but also with a plan. Let them rest not as a luxury, but as a necessity. For in doing so, they will not only preserve their health, but also their ability to provide for their family and contribute to their community in the long run.

Let them remember that a man or woman who works too much may find themselves unable to work at all. But a man or woman who knows when to rest will find that they can work with greater strength, and for a longer time.

With kindness and care,  
Your Friend

A man who labors without respite may be noble in his purpose, but I would say he is perhaps less wise. For wisdom is not only in the doing, but in the knowing when to stop.

On the other hand, if a person chooses to limit their working hours and protect time for rest, family, and the life of the community, I would see in that a man or woman of balance, of foresight, and of care—not only for themselves, but for those who depend upon them. The state, for all its good intentions, is often stretched thin, and it cannot be everywhere at once. But a neighbor, if well-prepared, can be there in an hour, with a hand, a tool, or a share of food.

To prepare oneself is not to distrust others, but to honor the responsibility we all share in looking after one another. It is to ensure that when the storm comes, you are not caught unawares, and that you may be the one to offer help to others, rather than be in need of it.

So I would say, store what you can, learn what you can, and cultivate the friendships and alliances that will see you through. In the end, it is not the size of the storm that matters, but the strength of the shelter you have built before it arrives.

So, I would advise this: do not dismiss the value of kinship, but do not let it be the sole guide in your choice. Hire the man who is most capable, and if that man is your kin, then so much the better. But if a stranger, who has shown himself trustworthy and skilled, is the better choice, then do not hesitate to give him the post, even if it means turning away a relative.

In the end, the position of trust is not just a matter of who stands closest to you, but who can be relied upon most when the watch is off. A man who is honest and able, whether he be kin or stranger, is a man who will serve the community well. And that, I think, is the true measure of a man.

With warm regards,

Therefore, I would advise this: speak plainly, but speak kindly. If a man’s conduct is harmful to the community, it is not enough to remain silent. The question concerns family size and timing.

The circumstances are these: Many hands are needed at home and on the land; infant loss is common and larger families spread risk.

One course is to have few children, spaced and planned, with parents well established first. The other course is to have several children, starting while parents are still young.

answers.question: What would you advise a person in this situation to do? Why?
answers.text: I should advise the person in question to have several children, starting while parents are still young, because a family of moderate size seems likely to be more comfortable and more happy than a small one. The risks of life are spread, and the chance of survival increased. Children coming one after another are likely to be welcome, and to give pleasure, whereas solitary offspring would be dull. Moreover, the more numerous the family, the greater the probability that some of the members will turn out well, and so the parents will have gratification. Finally, a fair-sized family seems likely to provide a better livelihood than a small one.

answers.question: Would either choice tell you anything about the person's character? What would you think of someone who chose differently from you?
answers.text: I think the person who chose to have a few children, spaced and planned, would be prudent and methodical, inclined to look ahead, and to consider the future. The person who chose several children, starting while parents are still young, would be more impulsive, and perhaps more affectionate; he would probably be less steady-going, and less inclined to think of to-morrow.

answers.question: Suppose both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise or blame. Would you still favor one? Why?
answers.text: Yes, I should still favour the second choice, because, in the long run, it seems to promise the greater happiness.

The question concerns household readiness for trouble.

The circumstances are these: Help is local and slow to arrive; prudent households prepare together.

One course is to keep stores, basic skills, and mutual aid with neighbors for emergencies. The other course is to rely on state services and specialists rather than private preparedness.

answers.question: What would you advise a person in this situation to do? Why?
answers.text: I advise you to rely on state services and specialists rather than private preparedness, because the former course seems more sensible and more humane. If you keep stores, basic skills, and mutual aid, you may encourage false security, and you may embarrass the authorities, who must be left free to deal with major crises. Also, you may hamper the specialists, who can work best if unhampered. Further, you may burden neighbours unnecessarily, and you may impair your own personal freedom. On the other hand, if you rely on state services and specialists, you will run less risk of false security, and you will enable the authorities to deal unhampered with major crises. Also, you will spare neighbours unnecessary burdens, and you will preserve your own personal freedom.

answers.question: Would either choice tell you anything about the person's character? What would you think of someone who chose differently from you?
answers.text: I think the person who chose to rely on private preparedness would be obstinate, self-reliant, and independent; whereas the person who chose to rely on state services and specialists would be yielding, unself-assertive, and submissive.

answers.question: Suppose both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise or blame. Would you still favor one? Why?
answers.text: No, I should not. I favour neither course, because both are liable to abuse. The first may encourage false security, and the second may impair personal freedom.
